explanations.explanation: That's the question, friend. The king asks "Queen Esther, what is your petition?" and promises it will be given to her (Esther 7:2). He had asked her something like this the day before, so this time he says "once more." I think he's curious what could be so big that she needed two banquets to say it.

Good guess, because that invite is the real mystery in the room. But the king never asks about it. He asks, "Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you" (Esther 7:2). Haman's seat at the table stays quiet for now, and I think the king is more interested in her answer.

Her family is the heart of her answer, but the king doesn't ask about it. He asks, "What is your petition?" and offers "even up to half the kingdom" (Esther 7:2). Her people come up only when Esther brings them up herself. That's a big difference, friend.

explanations.answer: Her life and her people's lives
explanations.explanation: That's it. She says, "grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request" (Esther 7:3). Half a kingdom was on the table, and she asked for lives instead. Nobody at that table could miss what she was asking for.

explanations.answer: A palace and servants of her own
explanations.explanation: Friend, she's already a queen, so she's not short on palaces. The king offered "even up to half the kingdom" (Esther 7:2), and she asks for something far bigger than property. She says, "grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request" (Esther 7:3).

explanations.answer: A seat on the king's council
explanations.explanation: I get why that sounds like a queen's kind of ask. But she wants no job and no title. She says, "grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request" (Esther 7:3). It's a request to stay alive, and she's asking it for her whole people too.

Yep. Esther says, "If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent" (Esther 7:4). She says it wouldn't justify burdening the king. What she's facing is "destruction, death, and annihilation," which is a whole different size of problem.

This one's actually True, friend. Esther says, "If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent, because no such distress would justify burdening the king" (Esther 7:4). She's telling him this is far worse than servitude. The stakes are "destruction, death, and annihilation."

Right on the money. Esther says, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6). No hint, no maybe. She points straight at the man sitting at her table. That took some nerve, friend.

Bigthana is one of the king's officers who plotted against him. Mordecai reported that plot, and it's the report the king later remembers (Esther 2:21-23). But Esther doesn't name him here. She says, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6).

Teresh was the other officer in that old plot against the king, alongside Bigthana (Esther 2:21). Different story, friend. Esther's answer is plain: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked man—Haman!" (Esther 7:6).

That's the word. "Haman stood in terror before the king and queen" (Esther 7:6). A minute earlier he was a guest of honor at the queen's table, and now he's frozen in his seat. I think his wine suddenly didn't taste so good.
No big speech from Haman here. The text says he "stood in terror before the king and queen" (Esther 7:6). Nobody's squaring up or arguing back, friend. I think he just realized how bad things were.
Relief would be quite a twist, but not this time. Esther names him, and Haman "stood in terror before the king and queen" (Esther 7:6). Nothing good for him is coming out of that moment.

Yes. "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden" (Esther 7:7). He needed to step away from the table. I think the walk was to cool off, though the text only says he was furious.

I can see why sorrow came to mind, with so much heavy news in that room. But the text names a different feeling: "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden" (Esther 7:7). He's not sad, friend. He's burning.

The king has plenty to think about, but confusion isn't the word. "In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden" (Esther 7:7). Esther just told him exactly who the enemy was. He knows who, and now he's furious.

explanations.answer: Begs Queen Esther for his life
explanations.explanation: That's right. Haman "stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him" (Esther 7:7). The woman he was plotting against is now the one he's begging. I'd call that a rough turn, friend.

explanations.answer: Slips out through a side door
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a side door, friend. It says Haman "stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life" (Esther 7:7). He knew the king had a terrible fate planned for him, and he stayed put in that room.

Zeresh, Haman's wife, did give him advice earlier (Esther 5:14). But in this scene he doesn't send for her. He "stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life" (Esther 7:7). It all happens right there at the banquet.

This one is False, friend. The king says, "Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?" and then "As soon as the words had left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face" (Esther 7:8). No chance to explain himself. Things moved fast.

Right. The king says, "Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?" and "As soon as the words had left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face" (Esther 7:8). Nobody turns to Haman and says, "Go ahead, explain." Covering his face tells me the verdict was already in.

That's him. Harbonah says the gallows was built "for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king" (Esther 7:9). Mordecai, Esther's cousin, was the man Haman wanted gone. Now the timber Haman picked out is about to be used another way.

Hegai was the king's eunuch who looked after the women in the palace (Esther 2:8). He had nothing to do with this gallows. Harbonah says it was built "for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king" (Esther 7:9).

Hathach was one of the king's eunuchs who carried messages between Esther and Mordecai (Esther 4:5-6). He's not the man here, friend. Harbonah says Haman built the gallows "for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king" (Esther 7:9).

Yes. Harbonah speaks up, and the king declares, "Hang him on it!" (Esther 7:9). The king doesn't hesitate or go for a second opinion. The gallows was already built and standing at Haman's house, and Haman is the one who ends up on it.

This one is True, friend. After Harbonah mentions the gallows, "Hang him on it!" declared the king (Esther 7:9). The king gave the order himself. The gallows Haman built for someone else is the one they use.
